submitLabel: Your evaluation plan, the baseline data, and the write-up
intro: Paste the four baseline numbers with the query or report behind each, the change metric, the rework check, the kill condition with all four parts, your predicted count of capabilities with a pre-enablement baseline scored against what you found, and the 300–400 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, People Ops & HR Technology track — for People Operations, HR Operations, HRIS and HR Systems professionals who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 2 applied activity, 'The evaluation plan', for the decision they chose in Module 1. Five parts. (1) The four baseline numbers — volume, cycle time with time-to-first-response separated out, the repeat-contact rate, and the top five categories by count — each submitted as an ACTUAL NUMBER with the query or report that produced it, plus a stated population. The module's rule is that a baseline is a named query against a stated population on a stated date, saved so it can be re-run identically, and that a baseline taken after enablement is not a baseline. (2) A change metric that would move if things got better and would NOT move merely because people used the thing, plus the activity metric they are explicitly declining to report — naming the declined metric is a graded element. (3) A rework check: the tag, field or query that detects rework landing on employees, managers or coordinators, and who reads it weekly. The module's argument is that a deployment relocates rework onto people who are not the deployer, none of it appears in the project's numbers, and all of it appears in the learner's ticket queue, making that queue the function's rework detector. (4) A kill condition with four parts: a threshold computable from the Step 1 numbers, a date, a named person, and a rollback — including whether anyone has actually performed it and how long it took. An untested rollback is a hope. (5) The prediction scored. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS: reward actual numbers with queries over descriptions of where numbers could be found — a learner who submits three real numbers and names the fourth as genuinely unavailable, with the reason and what would have to change, should score ABOVE one who supplies four plausible-sounding figures with no queries. Apply the module's own test to the change metric: would it still move if the deployment made things worse for employees? Cost per contact and deflection rate both improve when someone gives up, so a learner who chose either without noticing has made the module's central error. For the kill condition, apply the sponsor test — could it fire while the project's sponsor still wants the project? A condition that names a committee and an escalation path rather than a threshold is not a kill condition. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that a deployment without a written kill condition is an installation with optimistic paperwork; its real counter-argument is that kill conditions are theatre because the organizational cost of reversing a visible deployment exceeds any threshold anyone would write, so the honest alternative is reversibility by design — small scope, one population, short window — making stopping a non-event. Note the counter-argument is built from Module 1's own rule that reversibility is the gate, so a learner who wants to keep both must explain what the written condition adds once the deployment is already cheap to reverse. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap. And where the learner genuinely cannot produce baseline data because they do not own the system or the reporting is inaccessible, that is a finding: score at full credit given a specific account of what was inaccessible, why, and what access would be required.

**"Our evidence cannot settle this" scores at full credit where it is the honest answer.** A submission that states plainly what its evidence cannot establish, and why, has done the exercise correctly — never mark it down for declining to reach a conclusion its evidence does not support. Reaching a confident conclusion on thin evidence is the error; naming the limit is the skill.

opening.label: Predicted — of your live AI capabilities, how many had a baseline before switch-on
opening.hint: From your Module 1 inventory. Zero is a common and honest answer.

calibration.label: Actual — how many you could evidence
calibration.hint: Evidence means a query or report you can re-run, not a recollection.

dimensions.name: The baseline is data, not a description
dimensions.criteria: The four numbers must be submitted as actual values with the query, report name, or system path that produced each, plus the population they cover. Descriptions of where the data lives score low regardless of how precise they sound. A learner who submits three real numbers and identifies the fourth as genuinely unavailable — naming which, why, and what would have to change — scores ABOVE one supplying four unsourced figures. Credit separating cycle time from time to first response, since conflating them hides the interesting result.

dimensions.name: The change metric survives the module's own test
dimensions.criteria: Apply the test directly: would this metric still move in the desired direction if the deployment made things worse for employees? Cost per contact, deflection rate, containment, and ticket volume reduction all improve when someone gets a wrong answer and gives up — a learner who selected one of these has made the module's central error and should be told which mechanism defeats it. Top marks for a metric that detects a bad outcome, such as repeat-contact rate on affected categories or answer accuracy sampled against the governing document. Also graded: naming the activity metric they are declining to report, and why.

dimensions.name: The rework check points outward, at somebody else
dimensions.criteria: The check must detect rework landing on employees, managers or coordinators — not the learner's own supervision time, which is the HRBP track's version of this idea. Credit a concrete mechanism specified as in place BEFORE enablement: a case tag, a field, a saved query, plus a named weekly reader. Credit awareness that a fresh ticket about the same issue often will not trip an existing reopen flag. A learner who notes that this measures contacts rather than experience — the employee who gave up never appears — has understood the limit and should score at the top.

dimensions.name: The kill condition could actually fire
dimensions.criteria: All four parts, and the threshold must be computable from the Step 1 numbers rather than a sentiment. Then the sponsor test: could this fire while the project's sponsor still wants the project? A condition that routes to a committee, names an escalation path, or triggers only on an outcome everyone would already agree is catastrophic is a review date, not a kill condition. On the rollback, grade honesty above completeness: 'nobody has performed it, scheduled for the week before go-live' scores well; silence on the question scores poorly; 'documented in the runbook' without performance is the specific thing the lesson warns about.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: The predicted count of capabilities with a pre-enablement baseline against what could be evidenced, with an account of what the gap reveals. Zero-and-predicted-zero is a legitimate top-scoring answer if the learner explains what that means for their function. Accuracy is never graded — only the account. Plus a committed position on the module's claim that engages the real counter-argument: that kill conditions are theatre and reversibility-by-design is the honest substitute. A learner who keeps both must say what the written condition adds once stopping is already cheap; a learner who adopts reversibility-by-design instead must say how small the scope has to be for that to hold. Also credit the honest answer to the write-up's final question — whether their own condition would fire while their sponsor still wanted the project, and what they changed after asking.
